Image 4: What if your employees aren't the problem? 
What if your employees aren't the problem?
Contact Center Show
In 1982, General Motors shut down its Fremont assembly plant, notorious for poor quality, absenteeism, and dysfunction. When Toyota helped reopen the plant under new management, it rehired much of the same workforce. The results were dramatically different.Same people. Different leadership. Different results.This week, Amas Tenumah and Bob Furniss ask an uncomfortable question: Are we running our contact centers like the old GM plant?From rigid attendance policies and obsessive handle-time monitoring to requiring supervisor approval for a $50 credit, contact centers have built entire management systems around the assumption that employees can't be trusted.And when a handful of employees abuse the system, leadership often responds by creating another rule for everyone.Bob argues that the problem isn't necessarily the metrics. It's the absence of individual coaching and the unwillingness to address poor performance directly. He also makes a surprisingly radical suggestion about attendance policies that leaves Amas momentarily speechless.The conversation explores the difference between accountability and control, why blanket policies are easier than actual leadership, and what happens when rules designed for your worst employees eventually punish your best.Same people, different results: What the GM–Toyota Fremont turnaround teaches us about leadership and trust.The tyranny of the exception: Why organizations punish hundreds of employees for the behavior of a few.Coaching versus control: Why changing a system setting is easier than having a difficult conversation.When quality assurance becomes absurd: Bob shares a story about his son receiving a zero quality score despite providing excellent service.The attendance policy debate: Should three absences automatically cost someone their job, regardless of circumstances?The hidden cost of rigid policies: How rules designed to stop abuse can strip managers of the ability to exercise judgment.Accountability without micromanagement: Why trusting employees doesn't mean abandoning standards or performance metrics.Are your policies written for the employees you trust or the employees you're afraid of?Because eventually, the rules you created for your worst employees will be enforced against your best ones.And when that happens, don't blame the policy. Blame the leadership that created it.00:00 – Welcome and catching up00:59 – The Fremont factory: Same workers, radically different results03:10 – Why contact centers operate on distrust06:01 – Do employees really need constant monitoring?08:52 – Why leaders punish everyone instead of coaching a few11:32 – Bob's story: Excellent service, zero quality score14:00 – What would we change if we ran a contact center today?14:46 – Bob challenges traditional attendance policies17:31 – When company policy punishes employees during life's worst moments19:26 – Are we writing policies for the worst offenders?20:23 – Leadership matters more than another ruleThe Contact Center Show with Amas Tenumah and Bob Furniss challenges conventional thinking about customer service, contact center leadership, employee experience, and the future of the industry.Subscribe for conversations that question how we've always done things—and whether we should keep doing them.

Draft 57: Inside the Life of a CEO Speechwriter with Felicity Barber, Thoughtful Communications
Smart in Public
In this episode of Smart in Public, the Katie's welcome Felicity Barber, the woman behind the speeches for leaders at Lloyd's of London, the Federal Reserve Banks of San Francisco and New York, and BlackRock. Today she runs Thoughtful Communications, where she writes speeches, coaches executives for the stage and trains corporate teams in public speaking.As comms people, we can all appreciate how in those rooms one wrong word can move a market, so we asked her how speechwriting works behind the scenes. Most of her answer was about trust. A CEO won't believe the words on the page until they believe the person who wrote them. So Felicity gets in the car with them, gets on the plane, sits in on meetings and keeps showing up until the relationship is there.Why this episode absolutely rips:🎯 One sentence at the top of every draft. Before the speech starts, Felicity writes the key message: what should the audience think at the end that they didn't think at the beginning?🏦 Storytelling in finance. Felicity often starts a finance speech with emotion, which makes plenty of people in financial services squirm. Her audiences include retail investors and entrepreneurs just dipping a toe in, and they need to understand what big institutions are doing on their behalf.🎤 The audience outside the room. The people who matter most may never sit in the audience. Felicity writes for university students while making sure regulators and financial journalists get the points they're looking for.🤝 Speeches become the narrative. A good speech often becomes how the company talks about an issue for months afterward. That's why Felicity brings in internal comms, investor relations, and the press team early.🤖 AI and the speechwriter. When one of her CEOs went through a crisis this year, they called Felicity and a PR partner they trusted -- not ChatGPT. Sure, AI can build her a business spreadsheet, but in her perspective is that it also made the writing harder, because now writers scrub out AI-sounding phrases on top of corporate jargon.🚶 What CEOs get wrong on stage. One is pacing in front of giant screens like it's a 2007 iPhone launch. Another is announcing great returns with a face like the dog just died.🙅 Words to retire. "Excited." "Thrive." Let's face it, most people are just trying to get through the day. And then there's "we're all like a family," which tends to come up shortly before the layoffs.💰 Money insight: Felicity wants speechwriters to talk openly about rates, especially women in the field, and to ask peers what they make, because pricing in this industry is hard to benchmark. Her red flags with a new client are haggling over every line item and a CEO who has already gone through five or six speechwriters. That second kind of client is how you end up at draft 57.🔗 Find Felicity at thoughtfulcomms.com and subscribe to her newsletter for speechwriting and public speaking tips. What's Rarely Measured Matters Most
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide |  Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

Scott Roth
CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER
Scott Roth is the Chief Executive Officer at LegitScript where he sets the strategic vision, oversees day-to-day operations, and ensures the ongoing business performance of the company. Prior to joining LegitScript, Scott was CEO of Jama Software, a leading product development and risk management platform for companies building complex and highly regulated products. Over the course of his 20+ year career, Scott has held several leadership positions with high-growth SaaS, internet, and data companies such as Salesforce, ExactTarget, and Return Path. He is a committed volunteer in the Portland community and serves as the Board Chair of Portland Opportunities and Industrialization Center (POIC) and Rosemary Anderson Prep, an accredited college prep school, youth mentoring, and job training organization.
LinkedIn
Jaylene Kunze
CHIEF OPERATING & FINANCIAL OFFICER
Jaylene Kunze is the Chief Operating & Financial Officer at LegitScript, where she is responsible for driving profitable growth and operational excellence across the company while overseeing Operations, Finance, Accounting, Legal, and Compliance. She brings over 20 years of financial and operational experience, primarily in software technology and Saas across ownership structures. Prior to joining LegitScript, Jaylene held various leadership roles at Hexure, Uplight, and MWH Global and worked in consulting and public accounting at Deloitte. She has a strong track record of helping high-growth technology companies balance growth while scaling sustainably. She does this by building strong teams, enabling technology, and streamlining processes with a laser focus on key SaaS metrics and KPIs. Jaylene holds a BA in Accounting from Hillsdale College and is an active CPA in the State of Colorado. As an active member of the Denver community, she serves on the boards of A Precious Child and Titan Colorado and coaches youth softball.
LinkedIn
Chris Riggio
PRESIDENT & CHIEF REVENUE OFFICER
Chris Riggio is the President & Chief Revenue Officer focused on executing the company's strategic go-to-market initiatives, building a world-class global revenue organization, and fostering seamless integration across sales, account management, marketing, and customer success teams. He brings over 25 years of experience in Fintech, specializing in driving revenue growth for high-performing software organizations. Chris has held executive leadership roles at Confluence, Institutional Shareholder Services, and ICE, where he consistently delivered impactful results. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Economics, providing a strong foundation for his strategic approach to business. A passionate advocate for excellence, Chris prioritizes supporting LegitScript's global client base while inspiring individuals to achieve their best, both professionally and personally.
LinkedIn
Dan Frechtling
SENIOR VICE PRESIDENT, PRODUCT STRATEGY & MARKET INTELLIGENCE
Dan Frechtling is the SVP of Product and Research at LegitScript, where he leads product management, policy research, and data integrity across all business lines. Prior to joining LegitScript, Dan held product and growth leadership roles across B2B SaaS. He was CEO at Boltive, a privacy and security software firm he turned around and sold to new investors. Before that he was CPO/CMO and later President at G2 Risk Solutions, a payments compliance vendor he grew and sold to Verisk. Prior to that he was VP and GM at Hibu and a senior consultant at McKinsey & Co. Over the course of his career, he has translated complex regulatory and risk challenges into scalable products, and he is an active voice in the payments and compliance community. Dan graduated Summa Cum Laude from Northwestern University and with Distinction from Harvard Business School.
LinkedIn
Charley Shamaly
SENIOR VICE PRESIDENT, PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT
Charley Shamaly is the Vice President of Engineering at LegitScript, where he leads the teams that build the software and platforms used internally and by customers, and oversees IT, security, and DevOps. He brings over 20 years of experience delivering SaaS products powered by machine learning. Before LegitScript, Charley was VP of Engineering and Product at BlueConduit, building software to assess risk across water networks, and held the same role at Themis, whose platform connects banks, vendors, and fintech partners to democratize compliance. Earlier, as Global VP of Product Engineering at Urbint, he led the teams behind software that protects critical utility infrastructure. Across his career, he has built engineering organizations that turn complex risk and compliance challenges into secure, scalable products. Charley holds a BA from Baldwin Wallace College, an MBA from Cleveland State University, and an ALM in Information Science from Harvard University.
LinkedIn
Kristen Zervis
CHIEF PEOPLE OFFICER
Kristen is the Chief People Officer focused on enhancing the employee experience, building inclusive practices, and fostering a culture of transparency, accountability, and genuine care. With more than 18 years of experience in human resources, Kristen has held leadership roles across the HR spectrum—from talent acquisition and organizational development to business partnering and operations. Before joining LegitScript, Kristen served as Director of HR for U.S. Retail at Adidas and held senior HR roles at First Tech Federal Credit Union. She brings deep expertise in building high-performing, values-driven teams that align people strategy with business outcomes. Kristen earned her bachelor’s degree in Organizational Communications from the University of Portland.

general||\"jaylene kunze\" cfo legitscri.raw_content:
What's Rarely Measured Matters Most
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide |  Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

LegitScript is a Portland, Oregon-based internet and payments compliance company that provides services for merchant monitoring, platform monitoring, and certification in high-risk industries. The company also performs investigative analyses for government agencies around the world regarding cybercrime, and offers brand monitoring for intellectual property infringement. Some of LegitScript's partners include Google, Facebook, Amazon "Amazon (company)"), Bing "Bing (search engine)"), and Visa. LegitScript also works with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to monitor and investigate websites marketing FDA-regulated products.
LegitScript has been designated as a Top Workplace in Oregon multiple times in recent years and in 2019 was named to the Inc. 5000 list of most successful companies.
Founding
[edit]
LegitScript's founder and former CEO is John Horton, who was a White House aide on drug policy issues from 2002 to 2007. Scott Roth is the company's current CEO.
The company is a founding member of the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies. The NABP has written that it endorses LegitScript on behalf of the government agencies that license and regulate pharmacies and pharmacists in the United States, Canada, and other jurisdictions for use "by search engine advertising programs, Domain Name Registrars, registries, payment processing companies, social media companies, and other Internet platforms to ensure that Internet platforms operate in compliance with applicable healthcare laws and regulations, and are not utilized in furtherance of the illicit sale of unregulated healthcare products". In addition, some EU government agencies have referred to LegitScript as the "appropriate authority" to which rogue Internet pharmacies should be reported.
Although LegitScript began its monitoring primarily in the online pharmacy and dietary supplement spaces, the company has since expanded into other high-risk areas, including transaction laundering, gambling, illicit adult content, scams and fraud, cannabidiol (CBD), content that advocates for hate or violence, and more.
Domain name registrars
[edit]
In November 2008, LegitScript launched its registrar notification program and reported that it had shut down 500 "rogue" Internet pharmacies by notifying their ISPs and domain name registrars. In May 2010, the company released a report regarding over 7,000 websites displaying a forged pharmacy license, indicating that it worked with 11 different domain name registrars to shut down the websites. In late 2012, the company stated that it had worked with registrars to shut down over 35,000 rogue Internet pharmacy websites in the previous four years.
As of early 2013, several domain name registrars explicitly state in their terms of services that they suspend and lock domain names identified as rogue Internet pharmacies by LegitScript, and outsource their abuse point-of-contact on Internet pharmacy issues to LegitScript. The company has stated that it works with most domain name registrars, and, in late 2012, it began publishing data showing that the websites of rogue Internet pharmacies "cluster" around a small number of registrars that LegitScript says ignore abuse notifications. Several Internet pharmacy affiliate marketers have publicly discussed the importance of registering Internet pharmacy domain names with registrars that do not work with LegitScript.[citation needed] In submitting abuse notifications to ICANN-accredited registrars, LegitScript has authority to act on the behalf of government regulators in some countries, such as Japan.
Consumer protection
[edit]
In March 2010, consumer protection website SiteJabber announced that it would begin integrating LegitScript's legitimacy determinations into its Internet pharmacy ratings. In May 2010, the WOT Services announced a similar initiative in which LegitScript Internet pharmacy legitimacy determinations would be integrated into its reputation rankings.
Dietary supplements and designer drugs
[edit]
LegitScript maintains a Healthcare Product Legitimacy program that monitors whether "dietary supplements have been the subject of regulatory action, are considered unsafe, or are marketed as miracle cures" and that is also endorsed by the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy. In its advertising policies for healthcare and medicines, Google indicates that it uses LegitScript's healthcare product legitimacy program to determine which supplements and designer drugs should be restricted from advertising.
Anti-trust lawsuit
[edit]
Legitscript is the subject of an antitrust action by pharmacychecker.com, a website which provides and compares prices of drugs from licensed international pharmacies, and verifies the credentials of these pharmacies. Pharmacychecker.com alleges that Legitscript is engaged in a conspiracy to suppress the information it provides. U.S. District Judge Michael H. Simon ruled on January 3 2023 denying a motion by LegitScript for a summary judgment for a stay of discovery in the lawsuit, as well as affirming Pharmacychecker.com as a legitimate enterprise. 
International Internet pharmacy certification
[edit]
As of February 2013, LegitScript's website indicated that it had approved over 250 online pharmacy websites and documented over 48,000 "rogue" online pharmacy websites. The program is also endorsed by the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy.

An Internet Built on Trust
We envision a commercial internet that makes life better for everyone, where individuals and businesses can make informed decisions based on accurate information about who they are working with and what they’re buying.
That’s why we strive to be the most trusted advisers to inform businesses, governments, and the public about which commercial entities are legitimate, legal, and trustworthy — and which are not.
Experience and Expertise
LegitScript has been leading the charge for a safer, more transparent internet and payments ecosystem for more than 15 years — combining technology and data with a team of experts skilled in monitoring, certification, and investigations. Our work with the world's leading internet platforms, marketplaces, payments companies, and federal agencies gives us an unparalleled view of the commercial internet. Hexure Names Jaylene Kunze CFO
Bringing more than 20 years of experience to Hexure, Kunze previously served as CFO of Urbint, Uplight and Tendril.
Anthony R. O’Donnell //

(Jaylene Kunze, CFO, Hexure. Source: Hexure.)
Hexure (Colorado Springs, Colo.), a provider of sales and regulatory automation solutions for the life and annuity industry, has announced the appointment of Jaylene Kunze as its new Chief Financial Officer.

Laird Rixford, CEO, Hexure.
Kunze brings more than 20 years of experience in finance and accounting to Hexure and will be a key member of the executive leadership team, according to a Hexure statement. She will oversee Hexure’s finance organization. Brent Tuck, Hexure’s current CFO, will remain with the company moving into a new strategic financial role.
“Jaylene’s experience leading companies through times of growth combined with her leadership style made her a great fit for Hexure,” comments Laird Rixford, CEO, Hexure. “We look forward to her impact as we continue to build solutions that power digital sales journeys for wealth management, insurance and financial services products.”
Kunze previously served as CFO of Urbint, Uplight and Tendril. During her tenure at Tendril, she spearheaded the company’s acquisition of five companies that led to the formation of Uplight. She has a bachelor’s degree in accounting from Hillsdale College and is a certified public accountant. She is chair of the board of directors for non-profit A Precious Child and has been named to the Colorado Titan 100 list in 2022 and 2023.

Brent Tuck, Strategic Financial Advisor, Hexure.
Growth Journey
“It is an exciting time to join Team Hexure as we work to build digital sales solutions for the future,” comments Kunze. “I’m looking forward to joining Laird and the rest of the leadership team on this growth journey.”
“I’m grateful for the support of Laird and the Hexure team as I move into my new role so I can improve my work and life balance,” comments Tuck. “Jaylene will be a great asset to the team, and I’m excited to work with her as we at Hexure continue to drive toward our company vision.”

Hexure Names Jaylene Kunze as New Chief Financial Officer
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo., April 10, 2023 – Hexure, a provider of sales and regulatory automation solutions for the life and annuity industry, today announced the appointment of Jaylene Kunze as the company’s new Chief Financial Officer (CFO).  
Kunze brings more than 20 years of experience in finance and accounting to Hexure and will be a key member of the executive leadership team. She will oversee Hexure’s finance organization. Brent Tuck, Hexure’s current CFO, will remain with the company moving into a new strategic financial role to allow him to spend more time with his family. 
“Jaylene’s experience leading companies through times of growth combined with her leadership style made her a great fit for Hexure,” said Hexure CEO Laird Rixford. “We look forward to her impact as we continue to build solutions that power digital sales journeys for wealth management, insurance and financial services products.” 
Kunze has previously served as CFO of Urbint, Uplight and Tendril. During her tenure at Tendril, she spearheaded the company’s acquisition of five companies that led to the formation of Uplight. She has a bachelor’s degree in accounting from Hillsdale College and is a certified public accountant. She is chair of the board of directors for non-profit A Precious Child and has been named to the Colorado Titan 100 list in 2022 and 2023. 
“It is an exciting time to join Team Hexure as we work to build digital sales solutions for the future,” Kunze said. “I’m looking forward to joining Laird and the rest of the leadership team on this growth journey.”  
“I’m grateful for the support of Laird and the Hexure team as I move into my new role so I can improve my work and life balance,” said Tuck. “Jaylene will be a great asset to the team, and I’m excited to work with her as we at Hexure continue to drive toward our company vision.”
About Hexure  
Founded in 1995, Hexure provides digital sales solutions to the insurance and financial services industry across various lines of life insurance, annuities, retirement, and wealth management products. Carriers and distributors use its solutions to build customer-centric sales experiences, accelerate submissions, reduce paper processes, meet regulatory requirements, and improve in-good-order sales.

What's Rarely Measured Matters Most
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide |  Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

Lawyerist Podcast
Law firms spend enormous amounts of time and money winning new clients, then often overlook the relationships they have already built. In episode 636 of the Lawyerist Podcast, Stephanie Everett talks with EJ Stern and Katherine Wilson about how intentional client nurturing can lead to stronger relationships, repeat business, and more referrals. EJ and Katherine explain why clients can quietly disappear when firms stop staying connected, why asking for feedback can strengthen rather than threaten a relationship, and how lawyers can move beyond being the person clients call with one legal problem to becoming a trusted advisor they call about everything else. They also share practical ways to stay top of mind, from LinkedIn and personal check-ins to thoughtful gifts, memorable experiences, and small gestures that show you actually know the person behind the matter. As AI-generated communication becomes easier to produce, authentic human connection may become even more valuable. If your firm is constantly focused on finding the next client, this conversation is a reminder that some of your best growth opportunities may already know, like, and trust you. Image 4: What if your employees aren't the problem? 
What if your employees aren't the problem?
Contact Center Show
In 1982, General Motors shut down its Fremont assembly plant, notorious for poor quality, absenteeism, and dysfunction. When Toyota helped reopen the plant under new management, it rehired much of the same workforce. The results were dramatically different.Same people. Different leadership. Different results.This week, Amas Tenumah and Bob Furniss ask an uncomfortable question: Are we running our contact centers like the old GM plant?From rigid attendance policies and obsessive handle-time monitoring to requiring supervisor approval for a $50 credit, contact centers have built entire management systems around the assumption that employees can't be trusted.And when a handful of employees abuse the system, leadership often responds by creating another rule for everyone.Bob argues that the problem isn't necessarily the metrics. It's the absence of individual coaching and the unwillingness to address poor performance directly. He also makes a surprisingly radical suggestion about attendance policies that leaves Amas momentarily speechless.The conversation explores the difference between accountability and control, why blanket policies are easier than actual leadership, and what happens when rules designed for your worst employees eventually punish your best.Same people, different results: What the GM–Toyota Fremont turnaround teaches us about leadership and trust.The tyranny of the exception: Why organizations punish hundreds of employees for the behavior of a few.Coaching versus control: Why changing a system setting is easier than having a difficult conversation.When quality assurance becomes absurd: Bob shares a story about his son receiving a zero quality score despite providing excellent service.The attendance policy debate: Should three absences automatically cost someone their job, regardless of circumstances?The hidden cost of rigid policies: How rules designed to stop abuse can strip managers of the ability to exercise judgment.Accountability without micromanagement: Why trusting employees doesn't mean abandoning standards or performance metrics.Are your policies written for the employees you trust or the employees you're afraid of?Because eventually, the rules you created for your worst employees will be enforced against your best ones.And when that happens, don't blame the policy. Blame the leadership that created it.00:00 – Welcome and catching up00:59 – The Fremont factory: Same workers, radically different results03:10 – Why contact centers operate on distrust06:01 – Do employees really need constant monitoring?08:52 – Why leaders punish everyone instead of coaching a few11:32 – Bob's story: Excellent service, zero quality score14:00 – What would we change if we ran a contact center today?14:46 – Bob challenges traditional attendance policies17:31 – When company policy punishes employees during life's worst moments19:26 – Are we writing policies for the worst offenders?20:23 – Leadership matters more than another ruleThe Contact Center Show with Amas Tenumah and Bob Furniss challenges conventional thinking about customer service, contact center leadership, employee experience, and the future of the industry.Subscribe for conversations that question how we've always done things—and whether we should keep doing them.

Image 5: Draft 57: Inside the Life of a CEO Speechwriter with Felicity Barber, Thoughtful Communications
Draft 57: Inside the Life of a CEO Speechwriter with Felicity Barber, Thoughtful Communications
Smart in Public
In this episode of Smart in Public, the Katie's welcome Felicity Barber, the woman behind the speeches for leaders at Lloyd's of London, the Federal Reserve Banks of San Francisco and New York, and BlackRock. Today she runs Thoughtful Communications, where she writes speeches, coaches executives for the stage and trains corporate teams in public speaking.As comms people, we can all appreciate how in those rooms one wrong word can move a market, so we asked her how speechwriting works behind the scenes. Most of her answer was about trust. A CEO won't believe the words on the page until they believe the person who wrote them. So Felicity gets in the car with them, gets on the plane, sits in on meetings and keeps showing up until the relationship is there.Why this episode absolutely rips:🎯 One sentence at the top of every draft. Before the speech starts, Felicity writes the key message: what should the audience think at the end that they didn't think at the beginning?🏦 Storytelling in finance. Felicity often starts a finance speech with emotion, which makes plenty of people in financial services squirm. Her audiences include retail investors and entrepreneurs just dipping a toe in, and they need to understand what big institutions are doing on their behalf.🎤 The audience outside the room. The people who matter most may never sit in the audience. Felicity writes for university students while making sure regulators and financial journalists get the points they're looking for.🤝 Speeches become the narrative. A good speech often becomes how the company talks about an issue for months afterward. That's why Felicity brings in internal comms, investor relations, and the press team early.🤖 AI and the speechwriter. When one of her CEOs went through a crisis this year, they called Felicity and a PR partner they trusted -- not ChatGPT. Sure, AI can build her a business spreadsheet, but in her perspective is that it also made the writing harder, because now writers scrub out AI-sounding phrases on top of corporate jargon.🚶 What CEOs get wrong on stage. One is pacing in front of giant screens like it's a 2007 iPhone launch. Another is announcing great returns with a face like the dog just died.🙅 Words to retire. "Excited." "Thrive." Let's face it, most people are just trying to get through the day. And then there's "we're all like a family," which tends to come up shortly before the layoffs.💰 Money insight: Felicity wants speechwriters to talk openly about rates, especially women in the field, and to ask peers what they make, because pricing in this industry is hard to benchmark. Her red flags with a new client are haggling over every line item and a CEO who has already gone through five or six speechwriters. That second kind of client is how you end up at draft 57.🔗 Find Felicity at thoughtfulcomms.com and subscribe to her newsletter for speechwriting and public speaking tips. 1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
CFO THOUGHT LEADER7 Kesä
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

MD Integrations is partnering with LegitScript as an Enterprise Certification Partner, offering expedited certification packages to virtual care and telehealth brands seeking compliance as a competitive advantage.
NEW YORK, Sept. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MD Integrations, the only unified telehealth platform built on a nationwide, doctor-only network, announced a partnership with LegitScript. The partnership embeds LegitScript certification directly into MD Integrations' onboarding workflow, giving telehealth and virtual care brands a single, streamlined path to compliance, with Legitscript application reviews beginning in as little as two business days.
"In digital healthcare, every week of delay and non-compliance is a missed opportunity to serve patients and grow your brand compliantly in the virtual care ecosystem," said Dr. Marc Serota, Founder and CEO of MD Integrations. "By combining LegitScript's compliance expertise with our leading provider-led infrastructure, we are excited to deliver the most comprehensive and compliant centralized digital health solution for telehealth and virtual care companies."
"Telehealth founders do not have the luxury of choosing between speed-to-market and compliance. This partnership means MD Integrations' brand partners get both from day one. When certification is proactively built into onboarding, brands launch faster and pursue advertising with confidence on platforms like Google and Meta from the start." Angela Salter, VP of Enterprise Certification Sales and Strategic Partnerships of LegitScript.
An Embedded End-to-End Certification Path
As an Enterprise Certification Partner, MD Integrations now offers brand partners:
By combining the industry's most integrated, physician-only clinical infrastructure with expedited access to LegitScript certification, MD Integrations removes a critical growth bottleneck for telehealth and virtual care brands, delivering the rapid and compliant turnaround, reducing time-to-launch, and accelerating brands' path to revenue and scale.
Seamless Integration
As an Enterprise Certification Partner, MD Integrations embeds LegitScript certification directly into its onboarding process, enabling a connected workflow for LegitScript certification. Through MD Integrations, brands can seamlessly apply for LegitScript certification and have questions addressed through a centralized source and streamline input.
Clinician-Led, Compliance-First by Design
MD Integrations' approach to certification is anchored in the same physician-led model that underpins its clinical network. Because the MD Integrations platform is built and operated with real-world clinical and regulatory expertise from board-certified MDs and DOs, compliance is treated as a foundational part of the infrastructure rather than a separate function layered on top. That same expertise now extends directly into how brand partners navigate LegitScript certification.
About MD Integrations
MD Integrations is a clinical infrastructure company powering a physician-only network of board-certified MDs and DOs across all 50 US states, DC, Puerto Rico, Guam and Canada.   
MD Integrations partners with more than 200 healthcare brands across specialties including weight management, longevity, women's health, and dermatology, giving founders and operators the clinical backbone to launch and scale compliant telehealth services without building physician networks or clinical infrastructure from scratch. Learn more about our partnership and MD Integrations at www.mdintegrations.com.

Meant Launches LegitScript-Certified GLP-1 Telehealth Platform with Coaching
News
Meant Launches LegitScript-Certified GLP-1 Telehealth Platform with Coaching
  By Jon Napitupulu
 August 16, 2026
The GLP-1 telehealth market has expanded fast enough that certification has become a differentiator, and Meant is leaning on that directly. The platform launched this week with LegitScript certification, a credential governed by nine core compliance and patient-safety standards that also unlocks advertising access on Google, Meta, and other major platforms. For a new entrant competing against a crowded field of GLP-1 weight-care programs, that certification is less a quality badge than a commercial prerequisite, and Meant is building its early brand identity around it.
The clinical architecture is worth examining. Meant itself does not diagnose or prescribe. Prescribing authority sits entirely with OpenLoop Health, whose licensed providers cover all 50 states and hold the final call on whether a patient qualifies. That separation matters from a regulatory standpoint: it keeps Meant positioned as a technology and coaching layer rather than a medical practice, which carries different liability and licensing implications. Patients who do not qualify for a GLP-1, which includes tirzepatide (Zepbound) and semaglutide (Wegovy) among the approved options, still receive coaching and the supplement kit. Nothing in the program, the platform is careful to note, is automatic.
The bundled model deserves scrutiny. Pairing a prescription pathway with a proprietary supplement kit creates an obvious margin question: the kit is included in every plan, meaning patients pay for it regardless of clinical need. That design generates a recurring revenue stream tied to enrollment rather than outcomes. Whether the coaching component delivers measurable retention or adherence improvement is the actual clinical question here, and Meant has not published data on either. The supplement kit remains, at this stage, more of a product-bundling decision than an evidence-backed intervention.
What Meant represents structurally is a bet that compliance credentialing plus wraparound support, delivered cleanly through telehealth, can carve out a durable position in a market where providers and payers are increasingly scrutinizing which platforms maintain actual oversight versus which ones simply move prescriptions. The real test will be whether OpenLoop’s prescribing data, accumulated across Meant’s patient population, eventually surfaces outcomes that justify the coaching premium or quietly gets folded into a larger clinical network’s aggregate numbers.

LegitScript Healthcare Merchant Certification Terms and Conditions
This agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into by LegitScript LLC (“LegitScript”) and applicant, which seeks to be certified as a healthcare merchant or advertiser (“Applicant”).
By clicking “Agree,” Applicant understands and agrees to be bound by this Agreement, LegitScript’s International Healthcare Merchant Standards (“Standards”), and any LegitScript policy such as LegitScript’s Applicant Certification FAQs. Failure to provide payment or abide by these terms and conditions will result in LegitScript declining to approve or revoking any previous approval of Applicant. Applicant understands and acknowledges that applying for LegitScript certification is a voluntary process. Applicant agrees to be bound by LegitScript’s interpretation of the Standards, these Terms and Conditions, and Applicable Laws (as defined below) and, if certified, agrees to remain in compliance with the Standards and not pose a reputational risk to LegitScript, as determined by LegitScript in its sole discretion, for the duration of the certification period.
General Requirements
Compliance with Applicable Laws
Applicant agrees to advertise, offer, and distribute its products and services in compliance with all applicable laws, rules, telemedicine technological requirements, and regulations (“Applicable Laws”). Applicable Laws shall be broadly defined and include, but shall not be limited to, the laws, rules, guidance documents, board statements, regulations, and telemedicine technological requirements of any jurisdiction where Applicant is domiciled, any jurisdiction where Applicant or its employees or agents maintains a pharmacy, medical or other license, and any jurisdiction where the Applicant offers to do business, including, but not limited to, the distribution of products or provision of services to patients or customers and where any existing or prospective customer is located. Applicant further agrees to adhere to generally accepted standards of ethics, medicine, pharmacy and other healthcare practices in all jurisdictions where Applicant distributes products or conducts services.
Accuracy of Information
Applicant represents and warrants that all information provided to LegitScript by Applicant is and will be truthful, accurate, and not misleading. Failure to provide full and accurate answers, (inclusive of all past and present communication with LegitScript whether related to a certification application or otherwise) as determined in LegitScript’s discretion, may result in a permanent denial or revocation of application.
Applicant represents and warrants that all information provided to the public on its website or websites is and will be truthful, accurate, and not misleading.
Applicant will fully disclose affiliates in the application. “Affiliates” is defined as any individual, business, or entity who previously, currently, or is expected to have a commercial and/or professional relationship with the applicant organization or its principals. The failure to disclose all Affiliates may result in denial or revocation of the application.
Intellectual Property Rights
Applicant represents and warrants that none of its information or business practices infringe any copyright, patent, trade secret, trademark, or other intellectual property right. Applicant agrees not to use any LegitScript intellectual property, including but not limited to LegitScript’s logo and Seal (as defined herein), for any purpose except as expressly permitted by this Agreement.
License
Applicant represents, warrants, and agrees as follows:
1. Applicant holds all necessary and valid license(s) from each jurisdiction required in order to comply with Applicable Laws. Applicant is in good standing to conduct business pursuant to the terms of any necessary license(s), and will maintain and conduct its business in accordance with the requirements of its license(s) in all relevant jurisdictions.
2. Applicant is in compliance with all Applicable Laws regarding provision of its services and distribution of its products. For example, if Applicant sells or distributes controlled substances in the United States, Applicant has a valid DEA registration in good standing and complies with all aspects of the Controlled Substances Act.
3. Applicant agrees to notify LegitScript within thirty (30) days of becoming aware of any change in status to its licensure, business, or regulatory status in any jurisdiction or its DEA registration (if applicable), including whether these statuses are in good standing.
4. Applicant agrees to notify LegitScript within thirty (30) days of becoming aware that it is the subject of any adverse or potentially adverse legal, ethical, government, or regulatory action related to its license(s), business or ethical practice, practice of medicine, or the dispensing of prescription drugs (“Disciplinary Action”). Disciplinary Action shall be interpreted broadly and includes, but is not limited to: suspensions, probationary statuses, reprimands, warning letters, consent agreements, and any communication from any medical board, Board of Pharmacy or other regulatory agency or organization, regardless of jurisdiction.
5. Applicant will, at all times, employ or contract with licensed pharmacists, doctors, or other healthcare professionals as required by Applicable Laws for the provision of its services. Applicant will permit regulated activities to be conducted only by those individuals licensed to do so, and then only to the extent permitted or required by Applicable Laws.
6. Applicant has proactively verified that all healthcare practitioners employed by Applicant (including but not limited to, physicians, physician’s assistants, nurses, and pharmacists) are properly licensed by the relevant regulatory authority in the jurisdictions in which they practice.
Prescribing or Dispensing Prescription Drugs, and Telemedicine
Applicant represents, warrants, and agrees that:
1. Applicant does not prescribe, facilitate the prescribing or permit the prescribing of prescription-only medicines without a valid prescription as defined by law, including the presence of a legitimate practitioner-patient relationship. Applicant also does not dispense prescription drugs to any human or animal without receiving and verifying the existence of a valid prescription for those drugs issued by a licensed healthcare practitioner. Except where expressly permitted by law or regulation, a valid prescription requires that the prescribing practitioner, or a covering practitioner, have physically examined the patient in person prior to issuing a prescription to that patient.

Major platforms including Google, Meta, Visa, and Mastercard rely on it to verify regulatory compliance before allowing healthcare advertising or processing. This page covers what the certification costs, who qualifies, and how USA Payments' official partner discount works.

Why USA Payments
A Decade Serving High-Risk Healthcare Merchants
USA Payments is an official LegitScript partner and a specialist in high-risk healthcare merchant services. We have helped medical spas, telehealth providers, online pharmacies, and wellness clinics navigate the LegitScript Healthcare Merchant Certification process, maintain stable card-not-present payment processing, and secure advertising access on Google, Meta, and other major platforms that require certification.
Healthcare merchants classified under MCC 5122 and MCC 5912 face a specific compliance challenge. Here is what certification changes:
 Without it: ad platforms reject healthcare campaigns and merchant accounts face holds, freezes, and terminations
 With it: Visa and Mastercard card-not-present (CNP) transaction compliance is satisfied and healthcare advertising access is restored
 Ongoing: LegitScript monitors your business continuously so your compliance standing does not lapse
Through our official LegitScript partnership, we pass discounted certification fees and expedited review directly to qualifying healthcare merchants. No markup. No conditions attached.
Eligibility
Who Qualifies for the Discount
Find your business type below. If you process card-not-present transactions for any healthcare or healthcare-adjacent service, there is a good chance you qualify for LegitScript Healthcare Merchant Certification.
Medical Spas
Medical spas offering prescription-strength treatments occupy a unique compliance position, part aesthetic, part regulated healthcare. Platforms and payment processors apply healthcare compliance rules to any service involving licensed medical professionals or prescription-based treatments.
 You may qualify if:
 You process card-not-present transactions for medical aesthetic treatments that involve licensed healthcare professionals, such as injectables, dermal fillers, hormone therapy, weight loss treatments, or prescription-strength skin care
 You want to advertise services that fall under regulated healthcare or telemedicine policies on platforms like Google, Meta, or LinkedIn
 You want to reduce the risk of merchant account freezes, payment holds, or shutdowns related to processing payments for regulated services
 You operate across states or countries where certification is required for healthcare advertising or card-not-present payment processing
 You likely do not need certification if:
 You provide only non-medical cosmetic services that do not involve licensed healthcare professionals or regulated medical products
 You do not offer or advertise any prescription-based treatments, in-person or via telemedicine
 You operate only in markets or on platforms where certification is not a requirement for your services
 Your payment processing covers only non-regulated services not subject to healthcare compliance reviews
 Not sure if your business qualifies? A USA Payments specialist will confirm within 24 hours.
Check My Eligibility
Telemedicine Providers
Telemedicine providers that diagnose, treat, or prescribe through licensed professionals are treated as high-risk merchants by advertising platforms and payment processors. Certification is what unlocks stable processing and advertising access in this category.
 You may qualify if:
 You process card-not-present transactions for medical aesthetic treatments that involve licensed healthcare professionals, such as injectables, dermal fillers, hormone therapy, weight loss treatments, or prescription-strength skin care
 You want to advertise services that fall under regulated healthcare or telemedicine policies on platforms like Google, Meta, or LinkedIn
 You want to reduce the risk of merchant account freezes, payment holds, or shutdowns related to processing payments for regulated services
 You operate across states or countries where certification is required for healthcare advertising or card-not-present payment processing
 You likely do not need certification if:
 You provide only non-medical cosmetic services that do not involve licensed healthcare professionals or regulated medical products
 You do not offer or advertise any prescription-based treatments, in-person or via telemedicine
 You operate only in markets or on platforms where certification is not a requirement for your services
 Your payment processing covers only non-regulated services not subject to healthcare compliance reviews
 Not sure if your business qualifies? A USA Payments specialist will confirm within 24 hours.
Check My Eligibility
Pharmacies
Online and brick-and-mortar pharmacies selling prescription medications face some of the strictest advertising and payment processing requirements of any healthcare category. Certification is the recognized compliance standard across every major platform and card network.
 You may qualify if:
 You operate an online or brick-and-mortar pharmacy that sells prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or both
 You want to advertise pharmacy services or prescription drug products on platforms like Google, Meta, Microsoft Bing, LinkedIn, or TikTok
 You want to protect your merchant account from payment holds, account freezes, or shutdowns related to healthcare compliance
 You serve customers in the United States or other countries where LegitScript Certification is required by advertising or payment platforms
 You likely do not need certification if:
 You sell only over-the-counter products, are not licensed as a pharmacy, and do not process card-not-present transactions for regulated healthcare services
 You do not advertise pharmacy services or prescription products on any platform that requires LegitScript Certification
 You operate solely in regions where certification is not a platform or regulatory requirement for your services
 Your payment processing is limited to non-regulated products not subject to healthcare compliance reviews
 Not sure if your business qualifies? A USA Payments specialist will confirm within 24 hours.
Check My Eligibility
Digital Health Platforms
Digital health platforms sit in a specific compliance category: businesses that facilitate prescription medicine sales through contracted providers and pharmacies, without holding a pharmacy license directly. The qualification criteria here are narrower than other categories.
 You may qualify if:
 Your platform facilitates the sale of prescription medicines by connecting patients with licensed medical providers and contracted pharmacies, even if you are not licensed as a pharmacy yourself
 Your website processes card-not-present transactions for medicines that are considered prescription-only in the jurisdictions you serve
 You likely do not need certification if:
 You are an EMR or EHR platform that does not directly facilitate the prescribing or sale of prescription drugs
 You do not have a formal contractual relationship with the medical providers and pharmacies your platform connects users to
 Not sure if your business qualifies? A USA Payments specialist will confirm within 24 hours.
Check My Eligibility
Pharmaceutical Manufacturers
Pharmaceutical manufacturers, repackagers, and relabelers of prescription drugs or APIs operate under some of the most complex regulatory requirements in healthcare. Certification helps demonstrate compliance to advertising platforms, payment processors, and international partners.
 You may qualify if:
 You manufacture, repackage, or relabel prescription drugs or active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) that require FDA registration and cGMP compliance
 You advertise or sell prescription drug products on regulated platforms like Google, Meta, or Microsoft
 You export pharmaceutical products or APIs and need to demonstrate compliance with FDA and international regulatory requirements
 You are involved in virtual manufacturing or private-labeling and need to show that your partners operate under proper FDA registration and compliance standards
 You want to reduce compliance risks related to payment processing, advertising approvals, and regulatory oversight
 You likely do not need certification if:
 You produce only non-prescription or cosmetic products that are not regulated as drugs
 You do not manufacture, market, or sell prescription drugs, APIs, or controlled substances
 You operate solely for research, teaching, or analytical purposes and not for commercial sale
 You do not advertise or promote pharmaceutical products through paid media or online platforms

What happened to Kompliant?

LegitScript has deeper specialization in content monitoring; Gratify covers more stages of the lifecycle with compliance built into each.
